01 · What this is

What this is

This model was trained on every domestic flight out of New York in 2023. For any flight you set up, it estimates the chance of a late arrival and shows exactly which factors pushed that number up or down. Then it checks where the model is wrong.

Data

All scheduled domestic departures from EWR, JFK and LGA in 2023 from the BTS On-Time Performance data, matched with hourly NOAA weather at the departure airport.

Model

An Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM) adds up one learned curve per factor, so its explanations are exact. A LightGBM model trained on the same data is there for comparison.

Prediction target

The chance a flight arrives 15+ minutes after schedule. Cancelled (2.5%) and diverted (0.4%) flights were dropped, so it only covers flights that actually operated.

02 · Why it matters

Why it matters

Travelers rebook, pick connections and decide when to leave for the airport based on delay estimates. If the explanation behind the number is misleading, so are those decisions.

Is an explanation that's accurate about the model also accurate about the world? Evening flights look risky mostly because delays build up over the day, not because of the clock.
Do two methods tell the same story? The EBM and the SHAP-explained LightGBM pick a different top factor for about — of flights.
Who does the model fail? It's well calibrated overall, yet over-warns in bad weather and gives flights that end up 3+ hours late only about a 1-in-3 chance.

10 · Limits & responsible use

Limitations

What the model doesn't see

  • The inbound aircraft. Late-arriving aircraft are one of the largest causes of delay. The data only covers departures from New York, so the plane's previous leg is invisible.
  • Destination weather, air-traffic programs, crew legality, mechanical issues. None are in the data.
  • Cancellations. These are excluded, so the worst outcome for a traveler is not what the model scores.
  • One region, one year. New York's congested airspace in 2023. Nothing here transfers automatically to other airports or years.
  • Thin categories. Hawaiian Airlines (362 flights, essentially one long-haul route) gets the largest airline effect, from a tiny sample.

Suggestions for use

  • Show a probability with context (an icon array, the average flight), not a binary “will be delayed.”
  • Label counterfactuals as model sensitivity, not advice, and don't imply the traveler is responsible for systemic delays.
  • Don't use airline-level effects to rank or shame carriers. Routes, hubs and schedules confound them.
  • Publish group-level calibration alongside any deployed model, and re-audit when seasons or schedules change.
  • When explainers disagree, say so rather than picking the story that sounds best.
11 · Method

Method

AUC: probability the model ranks a random late flight above a random on-time one (0.5 = coin flip). Brier: mean squared error of the probability (lower is better); predicting the base rate for everyone scores . The EBM performs about the same as LightGBM here.

Data

Source: U.S. DOT Bureau of Transportation Statistics, Reporting Carrier On-Time Performance, all scheduled domestic departures from EWR, JFK and LGA, Jan–Dec 2023 (435,352 flights), with hourly NOAA ISD weather at each departure airport. Both were accessed via the open nycflights23 data package. Target: arrival delay ≥ 15 minutes. 10,738 cancelled and 1,796 diverted flights were excluded from modeling.

Features

At-booking model (7): airline, departure airport, destination (top 40 airports; others pooled), month, day of week, scheduled departure hour, airport busyness (scheduled departures from that airport in that hour on that day). Day-of model (+4): visibility, wind speed, hourly precipitation and temperature at the departure airport at the scheduled hour.

Models & validation

Explainable Boosting Machine (InterpretML; additive, no interaction terms, 4 outer bags) and LightGBM (600 trees, 63 leaves) for comparison. 80/20 split by calendar day, so the same day's weather and disruptions never appear in both training and test. Local GBM explanations use exact TreeSHAP. The model running in this page re-implements the EBM's lookup tables in JavaScript and matches the trained model to 10⁻¹⁶. Temporal-shift experiment: EBM trained on Jan–Jun without the month factor, evaluated on Jul–Dec.

Percentage-point view

In log-odds, contributions add up exactly. The percentage-point view shows, for each factor, how much the probability would fall if that factor were set to its average effect (zero) with everything else held fixed. These numbers are intuitive but do not add up exactly to the total, because probability is non-linear.
